details:
**Heart of Darkness**
Conrad's most famous work, an 1899 novella about a journey up the Congo River in the Belgian-ruled Congo Free State, drawn from Conrad's own 1890 trip there as a steamboat officer. Working for the ivory-trading "Company," the narrator travels from the Outer and Central Stations to the Inner Station to find the agent Kurtz. It was first collected in book form in Youth with "The End of the Tether."

**"The horror! The horror!"**
The dying last words of Mr. Kurtz, the brilliant ivory trader who has gone mad and set himself up as a god among the local people. Back in Europe, Marlow visits Kurtz's grieving fiancée (his "Intended") and lies to her, saying that the last word Kurtz spoke was her name.

**Charles Marlow and the Nellie**
Marlow is Conrad's recurring narrator, who tells the story of Heart of Darkness to fellow passengers aboard the yawl Nellie, anchored on the River Thames. He also narrates Lord Jim, as well as "Youth" and Chance.

**"Exterminate all the brutes!"**
The scrawled postscript at the end of Kurtz's eloquent report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs. Other Kurtz clues include the severed heads on stakes around his station, his membership in the "party of the unsound method," the Russian "harlequin" who idolizes him, and the manager's boy announcing "Mistah Kurtz—he dead," which T. S. Eliot used as the epigraph to "The Hollow Men."

**The "whited sepulchre" and the knitting women**
Marlow calls the unnamed European city (Brussels) where he is hired by the Company a "whited sepulchre." In the Company office two women sit on straw-bottomed chairs knitting black wool, like guardians of the gates of death. Marlow is hired to replace Fresleven, a Danish captain killed in a quarrel over two black hens. On the steamer Marlow later throws his bloody shoes overboard after his helmsman is speared, and the boat is trapped in a thick white fog.

**Chinua Achebe's "An Image of Africa"**
A 1975 lecture in which the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe called Conrad "a thoroughgoing racist" (in the original version, "a bloody racist"). He argued that Heart of Darkness uses Africa as "the other world," "a foil to Europe," and denies its African characters human expression.

**Lord Jim**
A 1900 novel about Jim, a young British first mate who jumps from the steamship Patna, which is carrying Muslim pilgrims to Mecca, when it seems about to sink. The ship stays afloat, and Jim is disgraced at an official inquiry. Captain Brierly, one of the assessors at the inquiry, later commits suicide, and in hospital the ship's chief engineer has delirium-tremens visions of pink toads.

**Patusan, Stein, Jewel, and Dain Waris**
Marlow gets Jim a post through Stein, a butterfly- and beetle-collecting merchant, at the remote trading post of Patusan, where Jim becomes "Tuan Jim" (Lord Jim). He falls in love with Jewel and befriends Dain Waris, son of the chief Doramin. When the pirate Gentleman Brown, helped by the treacherous Cornelius, kills Dain Waris, Jim lets Doramin shoot him. Part of the ending is told from Marlow's visit to Brown's deathbed.

**Nostromo**
A 1904 novel set in the fictional South American republic of Costaguana, centered on the port of Sulaco. The Englishman Charles Gould owns the San Tomé silver mine and backs the Ribiera dictatorship. During a revolution the trusted Italian dockworker Nostromo (Gian' Battista Fidanza) is sent to hide a shipment of silver, and he secretly keeps it.

**Martin Decoud and Holroyd**
In Nostromo the journalist Martin Decoud helps Nostromo carry the silver, is left alone on the Great Isabel island, and kills himself, weighing his body down with silver ingots. Sulaco later secedes as the Occidental Republic. The American financier Holroyd is the novel's emblem of extractive capitalism, and F. Scott Fitzgerald said he would rather have written Nostromo than any other novel.

**The Secret Agent**
A 1907 novel set in London about Adolf Verloc, an agent provocateur who runs a shop selling pornography and is ordered to bomb the Greenwich Observatory. His mentally disabled brother-in-law Stevie trips while carrying the bomb and blows himself up, and Verloc's wife Winnie then kills him. Other characters include the Professor, an anarchist who always carries a bomb strapped to his body, and Chief Inspector Heat.

**"The Secret Sharer"**
A story about a young, new captain anchored in the Gulf of Siam who secretly hides Leggatt, a fugitive mate from the ship Sephora who killed a crewman, and comes to see him as his "double." He tricks the Sephora's captain, then sails dangerously close to the island of Koh-ring so Leggatt can swim ashore, using the white floppy hat he gave Leggatt, floating in the water, to steer.

**Almayer's Folly and Tom Lingard**
Conrad's first novel (1895) follows Kaspar Almayer, a Dutch trader in Borneo who married Captain Tom Lingard's adopted Malay daughter. Their daughter Nina leaves with the Malay prince Dain Maroola, and Almayer is left in his unfinished house (the "folly"), turning to opium. Lingard recurs in An Outcast of the Islands, where he tells Peter Willems "Life is very long," a line Eliot also quotes in "The Hollow Men."

**Critics: Edward Said and Maya Jasanoff**
Edward Said's first book was Joseph Conrad and the Fiction of Autobiography, and his essay "Two Visions in Heart of Darkness" in Culture and Imperialism discusses the novella's imperialism. Maya Jasanoff's The Dawn Watch reads Conrad's life and works in the context of globalization.

**Other works and biography**
Conrad was born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski in Russian-ruled Poland, worked as a sailor, and only learned English as an adult. His other works include Victory, in which Axel Heyst is pursued by the hostile hotel owner Schomberg and burns himself to death after Lena dies; "Amy Foster," about the castaway Yanko Goorall; The Shadow-Line, in which Captain Giles helps a young man get his first command; and The Rover, about the old pirate Peyrol at Escampobar.
